 The paradox: Numerous hydroelectric dams in Da Nang are completely dry amidst the rainy season.
 Just when it seemed like the peak period for water storage and flood control was approaching, a series of large hydroelectric reservoirs in Da Nang city are facing a serious water shortage. In some reservoirs, the water has receded, revealing vast stretches of sand.
 Báo Thanh niên • 28/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 According to observations by Thanh Nien reporters at the end of October, a time when Central Vietnam usually enters the peak of the rainy season, large hydroelectric reservoirs in Da Nang such as Dak Mi 3, Dak Mi 4, A Vuong, Song Bung 4… are still experiencing severe water shortages. Water levels in many reservoirs are tens of meters lower than normal, causing significant difficulties in power generation.
 This paradox not only puts hydropower businesses under immense pressure regarding production and revenue, but also raises concerns about water resources for domestic use, production, and maintaining downstream flow during the upcoming dry season.
 The reservoir is dry, and the hydroelectric power plant is operating at a reduced capacity.
 At the Dak Mi 4 hydroelectric reservoir, specifically the section passing through the mountainous communes of Phuoc Thanh and Phuoc Chanh, the current scene is vastly different from previous years. Normally, by the end of October, water from heavy rains would have flowed in, the reservoir water level would rise, and the power plant would begin calculating and regulating flood releases to ensure the safety of the structure and reduce the risk of flooding in downstream areas. 
 The Dak Mi 4 hydroelectric reservoir is completely dry in the middle of the rainy season.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG
 However, this year, many areas of the lake have seen the water level drop significantly, revealing vast stretches of sand. Areas that were previously submerged are now open land where people can graze their cattle.
 Water shortages are also occurring at many other large hydroelectric reservoirs in Da Nang. Despite entering a period with typically significant rainfall, the water supply to these reservoirs remains limited, preventing them from operating as they normally would.
 Speaking to a reporter from Thanh Nien newspaper, a leader of Dak Mi Hydropower Joint Stock Company (which operates the Dak Mi 4 hydropower plant) said that in the latter part of the year, the committed electricity output according to the assigned plan is usually high, around 100 million kWh/month. However, this year, the amount of water flowing into the reservoir is too low, making it difficult for the plant to meet the committed output. 
 Cattle graze in the middle of the hydroelectric reservoir.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG
 Therefore, when the company's own electricity production is insufficient to meet the contract, it must purchase electricity from other sources to compensate for the shortfall. Meanwhile, the purchase price of electricity can be high, putting significant pressure on operating costs and business efficiency.
 "From mid-October until now, we have been incurring losses of more than 1 billion VND per day," this leader said.
 Water shortages not only affect the plant's production and business operations, but also pose a difficult challenge in balancing water resources for other purposes. When water reserves are insufficient, ensuring power generation while simultaneously meeting domestic and industrial water needs and maintaining downstream flow becomes extremely difficult. 
 The water recedes, revealing millions of cubic meters of sand.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG
 Concerns about water shortages during next year's dry season.
 In particular, if water levels do not improve in the coming months, hydropower reservoirs could enter next year's dry season with low storage capacity, increasing the risk of long-term water shortages.
 The leaders of Dak Mi Hydropower Joint Stock Company believe that in the current context, power plants must carefully plan their operations, balancing electricity generation needs with the requirement to replenish water reserves. Operation must not only serve immediate electricity production goals but also consider the needs of the population, production, and maintaining downstream flow during the next dry season.
 "Of course there are difficulties, but in the current situation, we have to accept and comply with regulations and directives. Most importantly, the amount of water flowing into the reservoir is too low, so the plant cannot operate normally. We have to calculate how to accumulate water again to prepare water resources for people's needs, production, and to maintain the flow to the downstream area of ​​Da Nang during the next dry season," said a leader of Dak Mi Hydropower Joint Stock Company. 
 A section of the Dak Mi 4 hydroelectric reservoir has dried up right in the middle of the rainy season.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG
 You may also like According to the leaders of Dak Mi Hydropower Joint Stock Company, one of the factors mentioned by meteorological and hydrological experts is the impact of the El Nino phenomenon, which can cause uneven distribution of rainfall between regions. In reality, some low-lying areas may experience heavy rainfall, but rainfall in mountainous areas, which are the main source of water for hydropower reservoirs, is limited.
 This means that the amount of water flowing into the reservoirs does not increase proportionally with the rainfall in the downstream areas. Therefore, even though Central Vietnam has entered the rainy season, reservoirs may still face water shortages if heavy rains do not occur concentrated in the upstream areas.
 Given this situation, reservoir management and operation units must regularly update weather forecasts, calculate water inflow into the reservoir, power generation capacity, and downstream water demand. 
 Areas that were once submerged under the lake have now become barren land, creating an unusual scene at a time when central Vietnam is usually entering the peak of the rainy season.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG
 "The principle is to operate appropriately based on the actual water availability, while reserving necessary water for essential needs during the dry season," shared a leader of Dak Mi Hydropower Joint Stock Company.
 Mr. Truong Xuan Ty, Deputy Director of the Department of Agriculture and Environment of Da Nang city, commented that the severe water shortage in many hydropower reservoirs during this year's rainy season is unusual. He believes this phenomenon is related to the impact of El Nino.
 Forecasts indicate that there may be 2-3 periods of heavy rainfall in the last 2-3 days of October and throughout November. However, the ability of water levels in hydropower reservoirs to recover still depends on actual rainfall, especially in upstream areas.
 Mr. Ty said that relevant authorities are currently closely monitoring rainfall, water flow, and water levels at hydropower reservoirs to proactively develop operational plans, ensure the safety of the structures, and balance water resources to meet essential needs.
 Below are some images captured by Thanh Nien newspaper reporters on October 28th showing a series of hydroelectric dams in Da Nang completely dry amidst the rainy season: 
 Limited water supply makes it difficult to operate hydropower plants, affecting their power generation capacity.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 The receding water revealed wide open spaces, some where people could graze their cattle or even pan for gold manually.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 Experts believe that the phenomenon of numerous hydroelectric reservoirs in Da Nang drying up is related to the impact of El Nino.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 In late October, instead of rising water levels, many areas of the hydroelectric reservoirs in Da Nang were left with vast stretches of barren land and sand. This contrast creates a striking paradox during this year's rainy season.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 At the Dak Mi 4 hydroelectric plant, wide stretches of sand appear in the middle of the reservoir. This scene contrasts sharply with the typical image of hydroelectric reservoirs during periods of heavy rainfall in Central Vietnam.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 You may also like Water shortages have also been reported at several other large hydroelectric reservoirs in Da Nang, including A Vuong and Song Bung 4.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 Water levels have dropped significantly at the Dak Mi 4 hydroelectric reservoir, particularly in the mountainous communes of Phuoc Thanh and Phuoc Chanh, revealing vast sandbanks in the middle of the reservoir.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 Not only Dak Mi 4, but many hydropower reservoirs in Da Nang city recorded water shortages at the end of October. Limited water inflow into the reservoirs poses many difficulties in maintaining power generation operations.
 PHOTO: MANH CUONG 
 Water shortages at hydropower reservoirs at the end of the rainy season raise concerns about the ability to store water for the upcoming dry months, especially for domestic use, production, and maintaining downstream flow.
